source: Yasunaga et al. (2024) Large language models as analogical reasoners
finding: Self-generated exemplars beat 0-shot CoT and fixed 5-shot CoT on math, but the margin over 5-shot CoT is small on GSM8K.
numbers: GSM8K GPT-3.5-turbo: 0-shot 75.0, 0-shot CoT 75.8, 5-shot CoT 76.7, self-generated exemplars 77.8. MATH GPT-3.5: 33.0, 33.9, 34.9, 37.3. PaLM2 MATH: 27.1, 29.8, 34.3, 34.8; PaLM2 GSM8K 60.8, 78.2, 80.7, 81.7. Row order read from garbled Table 1 text.
limits: Single paper, author-run, one prompt wording, 2023 models. Gains of 1 to 4 points; no seeds or error bars. GSM8K gain over 5-shot CoT is only 1.1 points.
agent_relevance: S3 variant: the recall step gives small gains on a mid-strength model; do not expect big wins on strong models.

source: Yasunaga et al. (2024) Large language models as analogical reasoners
finding: Method depends on model scale: weak models fail to self-generate valid exemplars; retrieved or fixed exemplars win there.
numbers: GSM8K by model (Table 4): davinci-003 5-shot fixed 50%, retrieved 54%, ours 61%; davinci-002 retrieved 47%, ours 48%; davinci-001 retrieved 11%, ours 9%; curie-001 all about 2-3%.
quote: with smaller-scale LLMs, the retrieved CoT performs better
limits: Only the OpenAI text-* family; cell mapping from garbled table. Crossover lies between davinci-001 and 002.
agent_relevance: Recall is only safe when the model really knows the problem family. Gate O7 on model strength; for weak models use given examples.

source: Yasunaga et al. (2024) Large language models as analogical reasoners
finding: On Codeforces, exemplars alone give a small gain; adding self-generated knowledge (a tutorial) gives more.
numbers: GPT-3.5-turbo-16k Acc@1/Acc@10: baselines 8-11% / 24-27%; ours exemplars 13%/25%; knowledge+exemplars 15%/29%. GPT-4: baselines 16-17% Acc@1; ours knowledge+exemplars 19% Acc@1, 37% Acc@10. GPT-3.5 with method (15%) about equals GPT-4 baseline (16%).
limits: Only 50 problems (level A, 2023), run twice and averaged; differences of 1-2 problems; no confidence intervals.
agent_relevance: Knowledge-first then exemplars is the better order for algorithmic tasks. Evidence is thin (n=50).

source: Yasunaga et al. (2024) Large language models as analogical reasoners
finding: On five BIG-Bench tasks the method beats 0-shot CoT and is competitive with manual 3-shot CoT.
numbers: GPT-3.5-turbo accuracy: word sorting 66.8 (0-shot CoT), 67.6 (3-shot), 68.4 (ours); logical deduction 30.0, 35.2, 36.4; temporal 40.4, 44.8, 58.0; colored objects 50.4, 61.6, 62.0; formal fallacies 53.6, 55.6, 55.6. A further row (75.2, 41.6, 57.6, 68.0, 58.8) is the knowledge variant or similar; label lost in extraction.
limits: Five tasks, one model; row labels garbled so some assignment inferred.
agent_relevance: Gains vs 3-shot are 0-13 points and task dependent; recall is not a universal win.

source: Yasunaga et al. (2024) Large language models as analogical reasoners
finding: Number and diversity of exemplars matter: K=1 is worse; K=3 to 5 is best; telling the model to make them different helps.
numbers: GSM8K/MATH by K: 1: 76.1/34.8; 2: 77.0/36.7; 3: 77.5/37.3; 4: 77.3/37.0; 5: 77.8/37.1 (mapping approximate). Diversity ablation: non-diverse 75.9/35.2 vs diverse 77.8/37.3.
quote: When K=1, the LLM underperforms due to excessive reliance on a single exemplar
limits: GPT-3.5 only; K to row mapping from garbled table.
agent_relevance: Ask for at least 3 distinct recalled problems, told to differ from each other and from the target.

source: Yasunaga et al. (2024) Large language models as analogical reasoners
finding: Manual error analysis of 100 GSM8K+MATH outputs: bad exemplars are not the main cause of failure; the generalization gap is.
numbers: 50 correct: 35 relevant and correct exemplars, 9 relevant but wrong, 6 irrelevant. 50 wrong: 28 relevant and correct yet solve failed (12 generalization gap, 8 overreliance on one exemplar, 8 other), 12 relevant but incorrect, 10 irrelevant. So 15 of 50 correct answers came from flawed or irrelevant exemplars.
quote: A common failure occurred when the LLM could not solve the new problem due to a generalization gap
limits: N=100, one model, authors graded.
agent_relevance: Do not trust recalled solutions without checking. Guard against anchoring on a recalled problem when the target is harder.

source: Yasunaga et al. (2024) Large language models as analogical reasoners
finding: Knowledge-before-exemplars order beats after; knowledge steers exemplars to the true method instead of surface likeness.
numbers: Codeforces GPT-3.5: knowledge after exemplars 14% Acc@1 / 27% Acc@10; knowledge before 15% / 29%. Without knowledge, the model drew palindrome exemplars, not the prefix-product method.
limits: One-point difference on 50 problems; the mechanism is shown by one worked example.
agent_relevance: Name the core concept first, then recall problems.

source: Yasunaga et al. (2024) Large language models as analogical reasoners
finding: Authors state limits: more output tokens, needs a strong model, prompt wording sensitivity.
numbers: Versus few-shot CoT: fewer input tokens, more output tokens. No token counts given. Contamination control: Codeforces limited to 2023 level-A problems.
quote: self-generation can fail if the LLM lacks sufficient strength
limits: No multi-seed or multi-prompt robustness study.
agent_relevance: Budget extra tokens for O7; test several wordings before trusting a gain.

source: Zhang et al. (2026) Learning Global Hypothesis Space for Enhancing Synergistic Reasoning Chain
finding: Independent head-to-head: Analogical Prompting was clearly worse than plain CoT on modern models across 8 benchmarks.
numbers: GPT-4o-mini EM%, CoT vs AP: MATH 78.3 vs 65.4; OlympiadBench 9.3 vs 6.5; GSM8K 90.9 vs 87.2; BBH 78.3 vs 72.5; MMLU-CF 69.6 vs 65.8; LongBench 57.6 vs 52.9; HotpotQA 67.2 vs 64.7; MuSiQue 34.1 vs 32.8; average 60.7 vs 56.0.
limits: Third party whose own method is the focus; AP prompt wording not stated in the part read; AP deltas nearly identical across backbones, may mean a shared implementation.
agent_relevance: Strong evidence against assuming O7 helps on current models. Treat as an option to test, not a default.

source: Zhang et al. (2026) Learning Global Hypothesis Space (backbone check)
finding: The drop of AP vs CoT has the same size on three backbones, so not a quirk of one model.
numbers: Average CoT vs AP: GPT-4o-mini 60.7 vs 56.0; Qwen-Turbo 60.4 vs 55.7; DeepSeek-V3 60.9 vs 56.3. MATH: 78.1 vs 65.2 (Qwen-Turbo), 78.5 vs 65.6 (DeepSeek-V3). GSM8K loss about 3.5 to 3.7 points.
limits: Near-identical deltas across models are unusual; no seeds or confidence intervals.
agent_relevance: Math is where recall hurts most (12 to 13 points); consider skipping analogical recall on competition math with strong models.

source: Islam et al. (2025) CodeSim: multi-agent code generation through simulation
finding: In a code-generation comparison table, the Analogical baseline (self-retrieved example plus plan) is usually at or below plain CoT, and well below simulation-based planning.
numbers: Pass@1 tables compare Direct, CoT, Self-Planning, Analogical, Reflexion, LATS, MapCoder, CodeSim on HumanEval, HumanEval-ET, EvalPlus, MBPP, MBPP-ET. Example reading: one block Analogical avg 64.8 / 59.9 vs CoT 67.7 / 67.2; later block 75.3 / 68.4 vs 77.1 / 73.2; strongest-model block 84.5 / 78.6 vs 86.8 / 81.3.
limits: Baseline reimplemented by authors; extraction garbled so block-to-model mapping is uncertain; numbers approximate.
agent_relevance: Plain recall of one example is weaker than checking the plan by simulating it; link to execution-based verification.

source: Ebouky, Bartezzaghi, Rigotti (2025) Eliciting Reasoning in Language Models with Cognitive Tools
finding: A 'recall related' tool inspired by Yasunaga helps, but is not the strongest single tool and varies by model.
numbers: Smolbenchmark accuracy, baseline to recall-related: Qwen2.5-7B 75.8 to 76.1; Qwen2.5-32B 79.6 to 84.2; Llama3.1-8B 48.7 to 53.2; Llama3.3-70B 52.8 to 75.1. Understand-question gives 78.6, 82.5, 59.4, 79.5. Average pass@1 over 16 repetitions.
limits: A tool inside an agent loop, not the original single prompt; only math-style benchmark.
agent_relevance: Recall works as a tool the model calls when needed, not as a forced step.

source: Ebouky, Bartezzaghi, Rigotti (2025) Cognitive Tools (tool use)
finding: When the model picks its own tools, it calls 'recall related' rarely and pairs it with backtracking.
numbers: Recall-related and backtracking each used about 20% of the time; Pearson correlation between their calls 0.18 on Smolbenchmark.
limits: Correlation is small; the 'recovery workflow' reading is the authors' guess.
agent_relevance: Recall is mainly a recovery move after a failed attempt. Place O7 after an impasse, not at the start.

source: Ebouky, Bartezzaghi, Rigotti (2025) Cognitive Tools (combined)
finding: All four tools together beat plain, CoT and code on hard math.
numbers: Qwen2.5-32B Instruct AIME 2024: 17.2 plain, 15.4 +cot, 19.6 +code, 32.1 +cognitive tools; average over AIME/MATH500/AMC 48.0, 48.3, 50.2, 58.9. Qwen2.5-7B average 42.7, 41.9, 42.7, 45.1.
limits: The gain is for the bundle; recall is isolated only in the Table 1 ablation.
agent_relevance: A bundle of cheap operators beats any single one; supports a schema with several operators.

source: Kim et al. (2022) Self-Generated In-Context Learning
finding: Earlier simpler idea: the model writes its own demonstrations conditioned on the test input. Works for classification and lowers variance.
numbers: Four text classification datasets; one self-generated sample worth about 0.6 gold samples; 8 self-generated samples beat up to 5 gold samples on SST-2 and SST-5; input-conditioned generation gives higher similarity to the input and higher accuracy.
limits: Classification only, 2022 models, no reasoning chains.
agent_relevance: Prior art for O7. Conditioning generation on the target input matters.

source: Zhang et al. (2022) Automatic Chain of Thought Prompting (Auto-CoT)
finding: Self-generated demonstrations carry errors and retrieval by similarity copies those errors; picking diverse questions fixes much of it.
numbers: Unresolving rate (share of questions still failed): similarity-retrieved demos 46.9% vs random demos 25.8% (128 questions). Auto-CoT 92.0 vs Manual-CoT 91.7 on first dataset; 47.9 vs 46.9; 84.8 vs 81.3.
limits: One or two wrong demos of 8 reported harmless; GPT-3 era.
agent_relevance: Recalled problems most similar to the target may copy the same error. Ask for diverse recalled problems.

source: Zhang et al. (2022) Auto-CoT (error tolerance)
finding: A small share of wrong demonstrations does not hurt accuracy; sampling one per cluster gives over 87.5% chance of 8 correct demos if errors sit in one cluster.
numbers: Claim: 1 or 2 wrong demos out of 8 do not harm performance; 7/8 = 87.5% chance of all-correct demos under single-cluster errors.
limits: Argument partly analytic, tested on GPT-3.
agent_relevance: Consistent with Yasunaga's finding that wrong exemplars often do not sink answers.

source: Min et al. (2022) Rethinking the Role of the Demonstrations
finding: Correct labels in demonstrations barely matter; format and input distribution matter. This helps explain why imperfect self-generated exemplars still help.
numbers: Random labels cause only a marginal drop across 12 models including the GPT-3 family on classification and multi-choice tasks.
quote: replacing the labels in demonstrations with random labels barely hurts performance
limits: Classification and multi-choice, not multi-step math; exact drop sizes not extracted.
agent_relevance: Part of the benefit of recalled problems may be format priming, not analogical transfer.

source: Wang et al. (2023) Towards Understanding Chain-of-Thought Prompting
finding: Invalid reasoning steps in CoT demonstrations keep most of the benefit; relevance to the query and order of steps matter.
numbers: Prompting with invalid reasoning steps achieves over 80-90% of the performance of valid CoT.
quote: CoT reasoning is possible even with invalid demonstrations
limits: Older models; abstract states relevance and coherence are key.
agent_relevance: Relevance, not correctness, of recalled exemplars may carry the effect; hard to tell from format priming.

source: Lewis & Mitchell (2024) Using Counterfactual Tasks to Evaluate the Generality of Analogical Reasoning in LLMs
finding: Failed generalization of LLM analogy: with permuted alphabets, GPT-3, 3.5 and 4 drop sharply while humans do not. In their run GPT models were also below human average on the original items, unlike Webb et al.
numbers: Humans stable from 0 to 20 permuted letters and symbol alphabets; every GPT model falls with more permutation and drops again on symbols. Webb et al. used 100 problems per type and 57 UCLA students. Overall accuracy numbers in the extraction are garbled and not cited.
limits: Letter-string domain only; temperature 0.
agent_relevance: LLM analogy may rely on training-data similarity. Recall of similar problems works best when the target resembles training data; expect failure on unfamiliar tasks.

source: Yu et al. (2024) Thought Propagation: An Analogical Approach to Complex Reasoning
finding: A rival analogy method: solve analogous problems first, then aggregate. Large gain on shortest-path with GPT-3.5, tiny with GPT-4.
numbers: Shortest-path 0-shot optimal rate: GPT-3.5 IO 0.33, CoT 0.26, ToT 0.22, TP 0.65; PaLM-2 IO 0.14, CoT 0.24, TP 0.36; GPT-4 IO 0.78, CoT 0.76 (TP near ceiling). 5-shot often no better than 1-shot.
limits: Synthetic graph tasks; extra LLM calls; 2-layer gain over 1-layer small.
agent_relevance: Another route to O7: explicitly solve neighbour problems and reuse. Gains shrink as base model strengthens.

source: Yu et al. (2024) Thought Propagation (creative writing)
finding: TP also wins on creative writing coherence and human preference.
limits: LLM-rated coherence plus small user study; authors' own method.
agent_relevance: Analogical reuse may help open-ended generation more than math.

source: Zheng et al. (2024) Take a Step Back
finding: Rival to analogy recall: abstraction (principles first) beats CoT and 1-shot on PaLM-2L, and CoT can even hurt.
numbers: MMLU Physics: base 66.4, 1-shot 64, CoT 65, CoT 1-shot 61.5, step-back 73.2. Chemistry: 70.9, 75.6, 75.3, 76.6, 81.8. TimeQA up to +27%, MuSiQue +7%.
limits: Different models and benchmarks; no direct head-to-head with analogical prompting.
agent_relevance: Abstraction step may beat concrete exemplar recall; compare on our own tasks.

source: Lee et al. (2025) The Curious Case of Analogies
finding: Mechanistic study: models fail to carry relational structure between entities in up to 38.4% of cases; patching fixes many.
numbers: Failures in relational structure transfer up to 38.4%; patching gave answer revisions in up to 38.1% of cases.
limits: Only the abstract and intro read; self-generated exemplars are cited, not tested.
agent_relevance: Even with a good recalled analog, mapping onto the target can fail.

source: Unlocking LLM Creativity in Science through Analogical Reasoning (2026)
finding: Cross-domain analogy prompting increases diversity and novelty of generated solutions versus no-domain baseline.
numbers: Solution diversity improved 90-173%; novel solutions over 50% of the time versus as low as 1.6% for baselines; applied to four biomedical problems.
limits: Abstract-level numbers; method searches distant domains, not Yasunaga's; LLM-judged novelty.
agent_relevance: Analogy recall helps novelty more than accuracy: use O7 for ideation, skip for exact tasks.

source: Which Prompting Technique Should I Use? An Empirical Investigation of Prompting Techniques for Software Engineering Tasks (2025)
finding: Tested 14 prompt techniques on 10 SE tasks, but its 'Analogical Prompting' means explaining with real-world analogies, not Yasunaga's method, so it is not a replication.
numbers: 14 techniques including Self-Generated ICL and Analogical Prompting; 10 SE tasks; 95% confidence, 5% margin sampling.
limits: Definition mismatch; no result for Yasunaga's method.
agent_relevance: Warning about naming: 'analogical prompting' means different things; do not count it.

source: Yang et al. (2026) Batch-of-Thought and other citing papers
finding: Many citing papers use Yasunaga only as related work; Batch-of-Thought even misdescribes it as retrieving similar cases.
numbers: Semantic Scholar lists about 100 citing papers in the first page; few run a head-to-head (found two: 2602.09794, 2502.05664).
limits: Citation text only.
agent_relevance: Citation counts are not replication evidence; true independent tests are few.
